flashcards.q: Define supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised anomaly detection and when you'd pick each.
flashcards.a: Supervised: labeled normal AND anomalous examples, train a classifier -- needs hundreds+ confirmed anomaly labels. Semi-supervised: train on NORMAL data only, flag deviations -- the common real case since anomalies are rare by definition (autoencoders, one-class SVM). Unsupervised: no labels at all, rely on structural assumptions like density or isolation ease.

flashcards.q: Why does isolating a point in fewer random splits indicate it's an anomaly (Isolation Forest)?
flashcards.a: Anomalies are few and typically differ from the bulk of the data on at least one dimension, so a random split is disproportionately likely to separate them quickly. Normal points, being numerous and densely packed, require many more splits before being isolated alone.

flashcards.q: Why does sklearn's IsolationForest default max_samples to min(256, n_samples) instead of the full dataset per tree?
flashcards.a: The original paper found a small subsample per tree is sufficient AND actually improves results by reducing 'swamping' (dense normal regions making isolation harder) and 'masking' (clusters of anomalies making each other harder to isolate). It's a genuine algorithmic choice, not just a speed optimization.

flashcards.q: What does LOF catch that Isolation Forest and z-score miss?
flashcards.a: LOF measures density relative to a point's LOCAL neighborhood (default n_neighbors=20) rather than the global distribution. A point can look globally unremarkable while being distinctly sparser than its immediate neighbors -- a local anomaly that global methods have no concept of.

flashcards.q: Why is OneClassSVM's default nu=0.5 dangerous, and what should you set it to?
flashcards.a: nu acts as your assumed contamination rate (upper bound on training margin errors, lower bound on support vector fraction). Default 0.5 assumes 50% of training data is anomalous -- wildly wrong for real scenarios (usually <1-5%). Set nu near the actual expected anomaly rate.

flashcards.q: Name three ways to set an autoencoder's reconstruction-error threshold, in increasing order of rigor.
flashcards.a: 1) mean + 3*std on validation set (three-sigma rule, inherits skew problems). 2) 99th percentile on a known-clean validation set (robust to skew). 3) Optimize directly on the precision-recall tradeoff against actual false-positive/false-negative cost, using any labeled anomalies -- the rigorous version production systems should converge to.

flashcards.q: Why is accuracy meaningless for anomaly detection, with a concrete number?
flashcards.a: At a 0.1% true anomaly rate, a model predicting 'normal' for everything scores 99.9% accuracy while catching zero anomalies -- accuracy rewards doing nothing because the majority class dominates.

flashcards.q: Give the concrete numeric example of why ROC-AUC can look strong while a fraud model is operationally useless.
flashcards.a: 1,000,000 legit transactions + 1,000 fraud (0.1% rate). A model with 1% false positive rate produces 10,000 false alarms -- 10x the actual fraud count -- but that 1% FPR barely dents ROC-AUC since it's computed against the huge true-negative denominator. Only ~1 in 11 flagged transactions would be real fraud even before counting recall.

flashcards.q: Why does PR-AUC not suffer from the same problem as ROC-AUC under extreme imbalance?
flashcards.a: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) has no huge true-negative denominator to hide false positive volume behind, unlike ROC-AUC's false positive rate which is computed relative to the (enormous) negative class. PR-AUC directly exposes how false-positive volume compares to true-positive volume.

flashcards.q: What is precision-at-k and why is it often the most operationally honest anomaly detection metric?
flashcards.a: The fraction of the top-k scored cases that are true anomalies, where k matches a human review team's actual daily capacity. Unlike PR-AUC (which integrates over all thresholds), it directly answers 'is this system worth the analyst time it costs' at a specific staffing level.

flashcards.q: What is the single most common reason production anomaly detection systems degrade silently over time?
flashcards.a: Missing human-review feedback loop -- flagged cases are acted on operationally but confirm/reject outcomes never get fed back into retraining, so the model can't learn from its own true/false positive history as the underlying data distribution drifts.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT use an autoencoder for anomaly detection even though it's the most flexible method?
flashcards.a: On well-structured tabular data with a modest number of features -- Isolation Forest or LOF typically match or beat autoencoder performance with far less engineering cost (no architecture choice, training stability, or reconstruction-error threshold calibration to maintain). Reach for autoencoders specifically for high-dimensional, unstructured, or complex nonlinear data.

flashcards.q: When should you use a supervised classifier instead of unsupervised/semi-supervised anomaly detection?
flashcards.a: When you genuinely have enough labeled anomalies (hundreds to thousands, not a handful) and the anomaly type is stable -- a supervised classifier with class weighting/resampling usually outperforms unsupervised methods because it directly learns the discriminative boundary instead of inferring anomalousness indirectly.
